newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland recasts ministries in government reform.
newsitem.headline: Poland recasts ministries in government reform.

text.p: Poland on Wednesday formally created two major new ministries and scrapped several others as part of a long-planned complex reorganisation of government, the government press office said in a statement.
Leszek Miller of the Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) party now heads a powerful new ministry of internal affairs and administration.

Miller was until now minister in charge of the Cabinet Office, a communist-era institution whose diversified tasks will be shared between Miller's new portfolio and a new chancellery backing up Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz.

Miller's fellow ex-communist Wieslaw Kaczmarek, until recently privatisation minister, takes over as head of the new Economy Ministry with responsiblity for implementing government industrial and foreign trade policies.
Apart from the Cabinet Office, the construction, industry, interior, planning and foreign-trade ministries are scrapped from Wednesday.
Barbara Blida, formerly construction minister, now heads a new housing and urban development office, while a Government Centre for Strategic Studies has also been set up.
Zbigniew Siemiatkowski, hitherto head of the interior ministry, now has responsiblity for the security service (UOP) which has been brought under the prime minister.

In an earlier stage of the reform on October 1, the privatisation ministry was scrapped and its functions taken over by a treasury ministry which went to Miroslaw Pietrewicz of the SLD's smaller coalition partner, the Peasant Party.

Disputes over posts in the newly-reorganised cabinet contributed to friction between the two coalition partners last year, but they were settled in October and the new ministers appointed on December 20.

Apart from streamlining central administration and granting more authority to the prime minister, the package has devolved some responsibilities to provincial governors -- who also took charge of about 1,300 remaining state-owned firms.
